title: Gradients, constrained optimisation and safeguards

objectives.text: Distinguish feasible global/local/stationary points and derive the convex first-order constrained condition, including a boundary optimum with nonzero gradient.
Derive and trace a bounded Armijo backtracking step for a stated quadratic, preserving the iterate on search failure and distinguishing acceptance/stationarity from a general optimum certificate.

blocks.markdown: An optimization problem specifies an objective f to minimize, a domain and a feasible set C. A feasible point belongs to C; a global minimizer has f(x*)≤f(y)for every feasible y. A local minimizer needs this only for feasible y in a neighborhood. A stationary differentiable interior point has∇f=0, but without convexity it may be a minimum, maximum or saddle. A solver exit status is not a substitute for feasibility, derivative correctness, objective meaning or a global-optimality argument.

For differentiable f, the first-order change along d is∇f(x)ᵀd. A direction with negative directional derivative is locally descending for sufficiently small positive steps that stay in the domain. In the chosen Euclidean coordinate geometry, d=-∇f gives slope-||∇f||²when the gradient is nonzero. It need not remain feasible under constraints. Coordinates with different units require an explicit scaling/metric; a bare learning rate is not invariant to changing the units of one coordinate.

A convex feasible set contains every segment between its points; a differentiable convex f lies above each tangent plane: f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y-x). For x∈C, the condition∇f(x)ᵀ(y-x)≥0for ALL y∈Ctherefore proves global optimality. Conversely, if the condition fails for a feasible y, convexity of Ckeeps x+t(y-x)feasible and the negative derivative decreases f for small positive t, contradicting optimality. This gives a necessary/sufficient condition for differentiable convex optimization, not a blanket certificate for arbitrary nonlinear constraints/objectives.

blocks.title: A constrained optimum need not have zero gradient

steps.text: Minimize f(x)=(x-3)²over0≤x≤1. Its unconstrained minimizer3is infeasible. On this interval f'(x)=2(x-3)<0, so increasing x decreases f.
The constrained solution is x*=1, with objective4and derivative-4. For every feasible y≤1, (-4)(y-1)≥0. The convex first-order condition holds despite nonzero derivative.

For a general target t on a nonempty interval[l,u], minimizing(x-t)²gives min(u,max(l,t)). If t is inside, it gives zero loss; if t>u, every feasible point is farther from t than u, and similarly at lwhen t<l.
A singleton feasible interval has only one possible point, whatever the derivative. This is a feasibility fact, not evidence that the unconstrained gradient vanished.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: 1 4 -4; 0 4 4; 1/2 0 0; then1. This helper solves ONLY one exact squared-distance objective on one closed interval. Clipping a general unconstrained optimizer is not a valid general constrained-optimization method.

blocks.markdown: Without convexity, f'(0)=0for f(x)=-x²but0is a maximum; f(x)=x³has a stationary non-extremum at0. In two variables x²-y²has a saddle at(0,0). Convexity can make a stationary point globally optimal; strict convexity gives at most one minimizer but does not by itself ensure one is attained on an open or unbounded domain. Nonempty constraints and a stopping tolerance alone do not establish existence.

A descent direction does not justify any step length. For f=(x-3)²at x=0, gradient=-6and d=6. Step t=1gives x+=6and objective9, unchanged from9; t=2gives x+=12and objective81, worse. Step t=1/2gives x+=3and objective0. Step-size choice matters even on a one-dimensional convex quadratic.

Armijo sufficient decrease requires f(x+t*d)≤f(x)+c*t*∇f(x)ᵀd, with0<c<1and positive t. Because the directional slope is negative, the right-hand side is below f(x). Differentiability gives f(x+t*d)=f(x)+t*slope+o(t); subtracting the Armijo right side leaves(1-c)*t*slope+o(t), negative for sufficiently small positive tprovided the domain allows those steps. Backtracking shrinks tby β∈(0,1)until this check holds. This local existence argument assumes a true descent derivative and an evaluable smooth neighborhood; it is not an iteration-count or global-convergence guarantee.

blocks.caption: Expected lines: accepted 3 1/2 1; stationary 3 0 0; line-search-limit 0 0 1. The fixed exact quadratic uses c=1/4, beta=1/2. At t=1the Armijo RHS is0while the candidate objective is9, so the first trial fails; t=1/2has RHS4.5and objective0, so it succeeds. A one-attempt budget cannot reach the accepted step and returns the original iterate, not a fake optimum.

blocks.markdown: The helper computes a SINGLE unconstrained step on one fixed exact rational polynomial. It does not run a general optimizer, implement projected Armijo, KKT multipliers or certify production risk allocation. A floating general implementation also needs finite objective/gradient checks, representable positive steps, domain/feasibility checks, evaluation/iteration budgets, tolerance/scaling policy and explicit search/gradient failure states. Projection changes the path and acceptance logic; do not reuse the unprojected slope formula blindly after clipping.

Record why a run stopped: small gradient under its chosen geometry, feasible projected-gradient/KKT residual when applicable, small step, objective-change tolerance, evaluation cap or failed line search. A tiny step can mean rounding or a bad direction; a small objective change can mean poor scaling. Assess feasibility and residuals against tolerances, compare analytic/small reference cases, and separate numerical stationarity from model validation and out-of-sample utility. No method here authorizes a live allocation or transaction.

Independent transfer: derive the interval optimum for target-2on[0,1], verify the feasible-direction condition and compare with target3. Trace the fixed quadratic step with initial t=2and predict rejected trials before code. Construct a stationary maximum and explain why a gradient norm check would miss the distinction. Specify what an iteration/evaluation cap should report without mislabeling an unfinished run converged.

References: [Boyd/Vandenberghe convexity and feasible first-order criterion, sections3.1.3and4.2.3](https://stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf), [CMU gradient descent/backtracking](https://www.stat.cmu.edu/~ryantibs/convexopt-F16/lectures/grad-descent.pdf), and [Stanford descent methods](https://web.stanford.edu/class/ee364a/lectures/unconstrained.pdf). Own fixed-quadratic code is standard-library only and makes no general numerical optimizer/runtime claim.

summary: Feasibility and the objective define optimality. Convex first-order conditions explain boundary solutions with nonzero gradients; safeguarded step acceptance, stationary status and search-budget failure are distinct from general convergence or model validity.
